cells.tense: The person stands where the false structure has already come down and the pattern underneath is clear.
cells.act: do the small practice again, alone, today
cells.ask: Do the same small practice again today, alone. Don't improve it. Do the plain version, same place, same time. Repetition is the point, not progress.
cells.core:
Things have come down that needed to come down, and you can see what's left. The shape underneath is the one that was doing the work. The clearing happened because something true arrived and stayed, and now the pattern sits where the clutter was.

Keep the small practice going. Not the version with a plan attached, the plain one you actually do: same place, same time, done again. Solitude here connects rather than isolates, and repetition isn't a cage. It keeps the pattern from getting buried again. Refine by doing it, not by thinking about doing it, and keep the light on through steady attention rather than one big push.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the pattern. Keep practicing it or it fills in.
cells.place: in the bare pattern under the surface of things

cells.tense: The person is bracing for the next thing to fall before the last one has even landed.
cells.act: join the practice the others keep
cells.ask: Join a practice the others already keep. Do it their way, not the way you'd overhaul it. Stay for the whole session and leave the redesign alone.
cells.core:
You're clearing before the clearing is finished. Something stopped holding and your reflex is to take the next thing down too, before anyone's felt the first one settle. From where you stand it registers as freedom; seen by the group, it looks like nothing gets to accumulate weight before it's gone. They've stopped bringing you the things they'd like to keep.

What's thin is contact, not restraint: being inside something shared while it's still alive. Join the practice the others keep. Do it their way, not your improved version, and stay through the parts that feel slow. Belonging doesn't require agreement, and a tradition that breathes does it by being handed on, not by being taken apart. The next ending you make will be the right one, and fewer.
cells.sheetLine: You're breaking ground before anyone can plant in it.

cells.tense: The person is still standing under a structure that came down and no longer holds any weight.
cells.act: give the mess a shape it can be carried in
cells.ask: Give the thing you're carrying one page, one place, one date. Use that once, and stop shouldering the old frame through another week.
cells.core:
Something is over and you're still holding it up. The frame stopped carrying weight and your arms are doing the work now. You've been calling that loyalty, or patience, and either way the load is real. Propping up a dead shape costs time something living wants from you, and it costs you the floor under your feet, so nothing new has anywhere to stand.

Make the smallest container that holds what actually needs holding: one page, one place, one date things go in. Not the perfect frame, the plain one. Leave the old shape alone for a week and watch whether it falls. That's the test. If it stands without you there, you didn't need to be there. If it doesn't, you've been carrying it.
cells.sheetLine: The frame is dead. Your arms are holding it up.
cells.place: in the bare pattern under the surface of things

cells.tense: The person is already in the middle of letting something end, while the pen sits untouched beside them.
cells.act: go where the feeling is already pulling
cells.ask: Follow the pull that's already there. Go where the feeling points, one afternoon, no plan attached, and notice that you chose it.
cells.core:
Something is coming apart near you and the hand loosening it is probably yours. Asked, you'd say you hadn't decided anything; the not-returning, the letting slide, the quiet non-renewal, all of that is a decision already being made. The pattern underneath is already in motion and you haven't signed the line yet.

Go where the feeling is already pulling you, one afternoon, no plan attached. Not away from the old thing, toward whatever is drawing you, because a move toward is legible to you in a way a fade isn't. The ending will keep happening either way; the difference is whether your feet point where you meant to go. That is the whole acknowledgment: your weight is on it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already letting it go. Put your weight somewhere.
cells.place: in the bare pattern under the surface of things

attempts.check: The strongest unsupported claim in the draft is that the person is actively clearing structures away, rather than that things happen to be collapsing around them; the record supports 'structure is moving' but not who is moving it. A reader could fairly say the collapse isn't something they are doing, and that would still be useful to them. The ask survives being wrong because it can be done whether the person is author or witness, and it teaches via the doing, not the diagnosis. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any phrasing that makes the reader feel the card has already decided what they have chosen to let fall, so that language has been removed.
